newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BAA eyes double digit growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BAA eyes double digit growth.

text.p: British airports operator BAA Plc announced a 3.4 percent rise in first-half 1996 profits on Monday and launched a new duty-free retailing arm, saying it hoped for double-digit earnings growth over the next few years.
Pre-tax profits rose to 304 million pounds ($501.1 million) from 294 million in the six months to September 30 on sales up 6.3 percent at 742 million pounds.
Earnings were up just 3.3 percent to 22.2 pence a share but the interim dividend was raised by 9.1 percent to 4.5 pence.
BAA said pre-tax profits would have been up 10.5 percent and earnings up by 11.1 percent but for a nine million pound exceptional gain a year ago.
It also plans to phase out seasonal fluctuations in airline charges, a move that had shifted 11 million pounds of income into the second half.

BAA said passenger traffic growth in the half-year to September 30 at its seven British airports was up by a weak 3.3 percent, reflecting a fall in European charter traffic and lack of spare peak summertime capacity at London Heathrow.

Finance director Russell Walls said BAA would seek double digit growth in earnings and dividends over the five years from April 1997, despite a slowdown in traffic growth and a multi-billion pound capital spending programme.

"The job that we have to do is to continue to deliver double digit earnings and dividend growth from a slightly more difficult base," Walls said in an interview. "Without making any forecast, that's what we are about to try and do."
Annual growth in passenger traffic was likely to slow to an average of around four percent, compared to five percent in the last five years, he said
Walls said BAA would try to boost retail revenues from the shopping arcades it has just finished building in all the major terminals at its British airports.

BAA also launched a new subsidiary on Monday called World Duty Free Ltd, to develop its duty-free retailing business worldwide and to take over next year the duty free shops at its own airports currently managed for it by Swissair.
BAA's first-half net retail income rose 10.7 percent to 224.5 million pounds as passengers spent an average of 4.20 pounds a head as they waited for flights, up 7.2 percent on a year ago.
"But we have still got only one in (every) two passengers who spend anything so it's a matter of getting more people to spend and to get those that do spend to spend more," Walls said.
Income from airport user charges increased by 1.8 percent to 283 million pounds and revenue from property rose 7.7 percent to 112 million pounds.

Meanwhile,Walls hit out at media reports that Britain's opposition Labour Party, should it come to power, would impose a "windfall tax" on BAA under its proposal to levy a one-off charge on former state utilities.

Labour says a certain number of utilities, such as water and power companies were sold off too cheaply by the Conservative government, leading to "fat cat" executives overpaying themselves and their shareholders with the proceeds.

Walls said BAA does not know yet if it is included in Labour's sights since the targets have not yet been named, but London's Financial Times said last month the company could face an extra tax bill of more than 500 million pounds.

"We will be making very strong representations as to why we should not be in the loop," Walls said. "We are not a utility, we are not a fat cat, we have not paid either special dividends or returned money to shareholders."

Walls said BAA has done everything the utilities should have done, investing heavily in the business with a multi-billion pound development programme underway including plans to build a giant fifth passenger terminal at London Heathrow.
"If they (Labour) take X hundred million pounds out of our pockets we will just have to say that is X hundred million pounds less investment," he said. ($1=.6067 Pound)
